design_detail: Editorial in The American Statistician (2016, vol. 70, no. 2, pp. 129–133) by Ronald L. Wasserstein, Executive Director of the American Statistical Association (ASA), and Nicole A. Lazar, presenting the 'ASA Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values', which the ASA Executive Committee approved on 29 January 2016 (statement printed on pp. 131–132). The editorial (pp. 129–130) explains why and how the statement was written: the Board's concern about the misunderstanding and misuse of p-values and about reproducibility; a group of more than two dozen experts with a wide variety of views, assembled by Wasserstein for the Board; months of discussion; a 2-day meeting of 20 members in October 2015; 3 months of drafts reviewed by group members, the Board and members of the target audience. The statement gives an informal definition of a p-value, six principles, a note on other approaches, a conclusion, acknowledgments and a brief reading list. Twenty-one commentaries by participants and others are listed as online supplementary material, which was not among the files read. A consensus statement by a professional body, not a systematic review: no search and no appraisal of studies; read with the editors' narrative-review checklist.
can_establish: What the American Statistical Association's Board, after a consensus process among statisticians with differing views, set out as widely agreed principles for using and interpreting p-values and statistical significance, and what the process deliberately left out.
cannot_establish: How often p-values are misused or misread in any field, or how much this contributes to findings that do not replicate (no data are presented), or where the participants who disagreed would draw the lines (their commentaries are in an online supplement not read here).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (consensus statement). Wasserstein, on behalf of the ASA Board, approached more than two dozen experts representing a wide variety of points of view, all of whom agreed to take part; 20 members met for 2 days in October 2015 at the ASA Office in Alexandria, Virginia, with a facilitator; drafts over the next 3 months were reviewed by group members, Board members (at the November 2015 Board meeting) and members of the target audience (p. 129). The acknowledgments thank 31 people (editors' count) and note that some of them hold views opposed to all or part of the statement (p. 132).
sample.selection_effects: The experts were chosen by the ASA's Executive Director; who drafted the text, and how disagreements were settled beyond leaving topics out, is not reported. The statement records only principles on which there was wide agreement: disagreements (multiple potential comparisons, how to describe alternatives to p-values, how much detail to give) are described in the editorial, and alternative hypotheses, error types and power were left out to keep the statement simple, which not everyone accepted (pp. 129–130).

outcomes.operationalization: Informal definition: a p-value is the probability, under a specified statistical model, that a statistical summary of the data (for example the difference between two group means) would be equal to or more extreme than its observed value (p. 131).

analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable. By design, the statement does not address alternative hypotheses, error types or power (p. 130).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Six principles agreed by consensus among invited statisticians, with an editorial on the process; no empirical data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The editorial says that nothing in the statement is new and that statisticians had raised these alarms for decades (p. 130); the statement presents its principles as widely agreed in the statistical community (p. 131). The empirical premises — that p-values are commonly misused and that misuse is one cause of the reproducibility crisis — are supported in the editorial by news articles, a blog post and a journal editorial banning p-values (p. 129), not by studies of how often misuse occurs.

timeline.event: Nuzzo's news feature on statistical errors in Nature, one of the discussions that prompted the ASA Board (as cited, p. 129).
The editors of Basic and Applied Social Psychology ban p-values (Trafimow & Marks, 2015, as cited, p. 129).
October: 20 members of the expert group meet for 2 days at the ASA Office (p. 129).

29 January: the ASA Executive Committee approves the statement (p. 129); it is published with 21 online commentaries and a guide to misinterpretations of tests, p-values, confidence intervals and power by Greenland and colleagues (p. 130).

replication.where_it_stands: The statement is the ASA Board's own judgment, published by its executive director with the participants' commentaries online. Its reading list cites a different 2005 paper by Ioannidis (JAMA, on contradicted and initially stronger effects in highly cited clinical research), not the PLoS Medicine essay on file as ioannidis_2005. For the site's 'Seven questions': it supports question 4 in that statistical significance does not measure how big or important an effect is (principle 5), and it warns against the shorthand that a significant result is probably not chance (principle 2); it bears on questions 6 and 7 through selective reporting and p-hacking (principle 4) and the weakness of a single p-value near 0.05 (principle 6), and on 'linked to is not causes' only in that significance says nothing about study design (principle 3). It says nothing about who was studied (1), measurements before use (2), doses (3) or absolute numbers (5).

funding.affiliations_note: Wasserstein is the ASA's Executive Director; he assembled the expert group for the Board and is named as editor of the statement on behalf of the ASA Board of Directors (pp. 129, 132); Lazar decided that The American Statistician would publish it (p. 130); the article's copyright line names the American Statistical Association (p. 129). Recorded as context: the statement is an association's position, published in its own journal.

what_would_settle_it: Not applicable to a statement of principles. How often each misreading occurs, and whether the statement changed practice, would need content analyses of published papers, abstracts, press releases and news stories before and after it.

domains.note: Consensus of invited experts; no search; a brief reading list is appended (pp. 132–133).
The principles rest on statistical reasoning rather than empirical studies; the editorial's account of misuse cites news articles, a blog and an editorial (p. 129), unappraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Neither the statement nor the editorial rests on the authors' own research.
The principles are framed as agreed principles; disagreements and omissions are described openly in the editorial (pp. 129–130).

domains.domain: Balance of views on p-values (dissenting and qualifying views are only in the online commentaries, not read)
domains.note: The acknowledgments say some contributors oppose all or part of the statement (p. 132); their views, and those of the 21 commentators, are not in the printed article.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a consensus statement (METHODS §5.3). The overall 'high' follows the rule that it can be no milder than the worst domain (no search) and does not question the principles, which are reasoning, not findings. Cite the statement as the ASA Board's judgment — for example, that statistical significance does not measure the size or importance of an effect, that a p-value is not the probability that chance alone produced the data, and that a large p-value is not evidence of no effect — never as evidence about how often these errors occur.

key_findings.finding: Process: the statement was prompted by concern that p-values are misunderstood and misused and by debate about reproducibility; more than two dozen experts with a wide variety of views took part; 20 members met for 2 days in October 2015; drafts were reviewed over 3 months by group members, the Board and members of the target audience; the ASA Executive Committee approved the statement on 29 January 2016. Its intended readers are researchers, practitioners and science writers who are not primarily statisticians.

Disagreement and omissions: the process was longer and more controversial than expected, for example over multiple potential comparisons and over the wording that a p-value near 0.05 taken by itself is only weak evidence; to keep the statement simple it does not address alternative hypotheses, error types or power, and not everyone agreed with that approach; there was high agreement that the ASA should speak out, and the editors state that nothing in the statement is new.
key_findings.locator: Editorial, 11th paragraph (p. 129, continuing on p. 130); 15th–16th paragraphs (p. 130)
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 4: the statement does not discuss power, that is, how large a study must be to detect an effect of a given size.

key_findings.finding: Informal definition: a p-value is the probability, under a specified statistical model, that a statistical summary of the data (for example the difference between two group means) would be equal to or more extreme than its observed value.

Principle 1: a p-value can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model, usually one including a null hypothesis of no effect or no difference; the smaller the p-value, the greater the incompatibility, if the assumptions used to calculate it hold; the incompatibility can be read as evidence against the null hypothesis or against the assumptions.

Principle 2: p-values do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone; a p-value is a statement about the data in relation to a specified hypothetical explanation, not about the explanation itself.
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 4 and says something different from its wording: the site's shorthand that significant means probably not chance reads a significant result as a statement about the probability of chance, which this principle says a p-value is not. Closer to the statement: data like these would be unusual if there were no real difference and the study's assumptions held.

key_findings.finding: Principle 3: scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold; a conclusion does not become true on one side of the line and false on the other; the design of the study, the quality of the measurements, external evidence and the validity of the assumptions must be brought in; the widespread use of statistical significance (generally taken as p of 0.05 or less) as a licence to claim a finding leads to considerable distortion of the scientific process.
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's questions 4 and 6, and on 'linked to is not causes' only in that significance says nothing about whether the design can show a cause.

key_findings.finding: Principle 4: proper inference requires full reporting and transparency; conducting many analyses and reporting only those with certain p-values (cherry-picking, data dredging, significance chasing, p-hacking) renders the reported p-values essentially uninterpretable and produces a spurious excess of significant results in the published literature; the problem arises whenever results are chosen for presentation because of their statistics, even without formal multiple tests; researchers should disclose the number of hypotheses explored, all data-collection decisions, all analyses conducted and all p-values computed.
key_findings.locator: Statement, 3. Principles, principle 4 (p. 131, continuing on p. 132)
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's questions 6 and 7: selective reporting is one reason a single significant result is a lead, not a fact.

key_findings.finding: Principle 5: a p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result; statistical significance is not scientific, human or economic significance; any effect, however tiny, can produce a small p-value if the sample is large or the measurement precise enough, and large effects may produce unimpressive p-values in small or imprecise studies; identical estimated effects have different p-values when their precision differs.
key_findings.note: Supports the site's question 4: significant does not mean big.

key_findings.finding: Principle 6: by itself, a p-value does not provide a good measure of evidence about a model or hypothesis; a p-value near 0.05 taken by itself offers only weak evidence against the null hypothesis, and a relatively large p-value does not imply evidence in favour of the null hypothesis, since many other hypotheses may be equally or more consistent with the data; analysis should not end with a p-value when other approaches are appropriate and feasible.
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 4, and rules out reading 'no significant difference' as 'no difference'.

key_findings.finding: Other approaches and conclusion: estimation (confidence, credibility or prediction intervals), Bayesian methods, likelihood ratios or Bayes factors, decision-theoretic modelling and false discovery rates rely on further assumptions but may more directly address the size of an effect and its uncertainty, or whether a hypothesis is correct; good practice combines study design, numerical and graphical summaries, understanding of the phenomenon, interpretation in context and complete reporting, and no single index should substitute for scientific reasoning.

reporting_issues.issue: Principle 3 writes the bright-line rule as p below 0.05 and, two sentences later, statistical significance as generally interpreted as p of 0.05 or less.
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the principles; a claim quoting the conventional threshold should not depend on the difference.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, with the publisher's unnumbered cover page as PDF page 1), pp. 129–133 (all pages: editorial, list of online commentaries, statement, acknowledgments and reading list; every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi). The online supplement (21 commentaries) was not among the files and was not read.
